Over a 64-second loop the coupling surges, drops out suddenly the way MMM's registers vanish, settles, and surges again; nobody is performing and nobody can intervene. At the side, a static panel: dark glasses, red rim-light. Beneath, the liner-note equipment list, deadpan as ever: no vocals, no melody, no overdubs, no applause. Energy music. Watch it feed itself.

title: The Deadpan
note: Reed's signature, stated as a picture: an extreme event, delivered flat. A Berlin-style spider crack spreads slowly across an olive duotone field, branch forking into branch for twenty seconds until the glass is a web; and through the middle of it, crossing the full width, runs one perfectly flat red line. It does not twitch when the crack passes under it. It does not brighten, dip, or comment. It holds for the whole loop, through the growth, through the stillness, through the fade, identical in every frame. The crack is the content; the line is the delivery. Watch-only, because there is nothing to negotiate with: the indifference is the performance, and it never once breaks character.

title: Ostrich Tuning
note: Lou Reed before the Velvets, on a Pickwick novelty record: every string tuned to the same D, the "Ostrich" machine he shared with Cale. Six horizontal strings span a near-black field, all at one fundamental, micro-detuned by fractions, and where their waves interfere, slow silver shimmer bands slide along the strings. A thirty-second loop: the strike, the drift as the bands travel, the settle back toward unison, a soft fade, and the strike again. There is nothing to touch and nothing to bend; the tuning is the piece, exactly as Reed built it. No guitar, no neck, no hands, just the lines and their beating. Watch it long enough and the shimmer starts to feel like weather inside a single note.

title: Not Bloody Likely
note: Wrong Way Up's cover as a choreography of friction. Two flat portrait busts hang head-to-toe on an olive field inside a border that repeats ENO/CALE in orange: the dark one upright above, the light one inverted below, noses nearly touching at the seam, a row of little daggers between them and purple lightning in two corners. Over a two-minute cycle they ease toward each other, hold at the closest approach, and ease apart again; they never touch, never align, never resolve, because the session never did either. Drag across a bust to flip it upside-down and rearrange the standoff yourself; double-tap reseeds both forms. No sound and no likenesses, just shapes at odds. Asked how the collaboration went, Cale's answer became the title of this piece. The daggers are load-bearing.

title: The Spinning Collage
note: For the Illusion LP reissue Cale collaged his own cover and printed one word upside-down; this piece obeys the same two rules: spin, and exactly one inversion. A big collage disc turns slowly at center stage, forty torn-paper fragments layered at rotations, eye-irises, lens rings, window grids, fabric stripes, in POPtical pink, vinyl turquoise and cream. Somewhere at the lower left, one fragment carries the word ILLUSION printed upside-down; find it while it circles. Drag to spin the disc by hand, fast or backward, and let it settle back to its resting turn. Tap and the collage shears for three seconds, vertical bands sliding sideways like a misregistered sleeve, then releasing. Double-tap reseeds the whole collage, new fragments, the word re-hidden. No sound, no photographs, nothing smooth: torn edges, flat ink, one mistake that is not a mistake.

title: Gothic Hypnosis
note: Cale called The Marble Index pitch-black pain, and this is its weather system. A low drone band of harmonium wood fills the bottom third and never drops out, two detuned saws breathing under everything once you tap for sound. Above it, three counter-figures, a viola arc, a piano shard, an organ haze, relate to the drone through a single changing attitude that the piece itself slowly drifts: coaxing, hugging the divider and echoing the drone's rhythm; soothing, rising into soft wrapping curves; then contrast, cutting diagonally at a tritone with ember flares, the quarreling mourners of "The Jeweller". Drag sideways to scrub the attitude yourself, from coax through soothe to contrast; double-tap reseeds the figures. There is never a melody, because the figures are postures, not tunes, and the hypnosis is in how long the dark holds still.

title: The Producer's Piano
note: The corrected fact as a piece: it was Cale who produced The Stooges' 1969 debut, and his signature on "I Wanna Be Your Dog" is one piano note, the same pitch, hammered on a rock-steady beat through the entire song, imposed on someone else's record. A dark studio; at center a vertical column flashes amber at exactly 100 BPM and throws a ripple across the floor, and it will never change pitch, never drift, never stop. Around it, slate riff-lines representing the band wander and dance but never touch the column; the pulse is untouchable and they know it. Drag pushes the band toward or away from the column (it will not reach); double-tap reseeds their tangle. Tap starts the pluck, the same note every beat, sharing one metronome with the flash. The band is chaos. The column is the producer. Guess which one the song is remembered by.

title: Between the Strings
note: The "All Tomorrow's Parties" session trick: paper clips wedged between piano strings until the piano rings like a small orchestra. A set of horizontal strings spans an ivory field, all on one pitch, and clips fall slowly from above on the piece's own schedule. Each landing perturbs its string: a kink travels down the line, a metallic shimmer settles around the clip, and the forest of perturbations grows, capped at twenty-four clips so the ring stays delicate. Drag across the strings to place clips yourself and cluster them into metallic chords; double-tap brings the sweep hand, clearing them left to right until the strings are clean sine again. Tap starts the sound, a soft pluck per landing, one pitch class only, because the clips are timbre, not melody. Preparation, accumulation, clearing: the instrument is the process.

title: All Strings to One Note
note: The Ostrich tuning, from Cale's months in The Primitives with Lou Reed: every string tuned to the same note, the guitar as a unison machine. Forty-eight vertical strings fill the frame, all vibrating at one frequency in perfect lock, their summed displacement glowing as a bright band at the center. The only event the piece allows: one string at a time slips slightly sharp, twenty cents of tension marked by an ember dot at its peg, beats against the field, and is pulled back into unison. Never two. Drag bends the nearest string sharp with your own hand and lets it settle home on release; double-tap drops the whole bank a semitone together, the field's color shifting with it. No chord ever forms. It is unison, or it is a brief, corrected mistake. The discipline is almost audible.

title: Any Song Has to Be Both
note: Cale's standing rule, the one Charli XCX saved in her Notes app: any song has to be both elegant and brutal. The piece enforces it as a strict alternation with no blending, because the cut is the content. For twenty seconds it is elegant: one thin sepia line drawing slow cursive arcs over moorland grey, and through it the ghost of a refrain in large quiet type, I think I'm gonna die in this house. Then, without warning, brutal: six seconds of red-black duotone clang blocks slamming the full frame, the refrain interrupted mid-word, gone. Hard cut back. Drag toward the top to extend the elegant, toward the bottom to feed the brutal; double-tap reseeds the arcs. There is no third mood and no fade anywhere. A door slamming is also a rhythm, and this piece keeps time with it.

title: Three-String Drone
note: Cale's master mechanism, built as an instrument you file yourself. In the Dream Syndicate he put a pickup on his viola and filed the bridge down, day after day for eighteen months, until the bow caught three strings at once. Here one beam spans the black, and one bright line rides it. Drag downward and you are filing: the line widens, separates into three detuned voices, white, smoke, amber, and the interference between them starts to beat and brighten, a melody rebuilt as a chordal drone. Drag up and it collapses back to a single string. The little pickup glyph rides the beam and glows with the total amplitude; the readout at the bottom is the luthier's caliper, bridge height in millimetres. Tap to start the sound; double-tap reseeds the pitches. The widening is the piece. Nothing else happens, and it is enough.

title: A Physician Should Be in Attendance
note: Conrad's master move, the paperwork as cinema. This piece is only its own paraphernalia: a warning card on paper stock, a title card, a card announcing THE FILM WILL NOW BEGIN, and then, where the film should be, a held black frame that breathes almost imperceptibly. Below, the projection booth keeps its ledger in amber mono: frame count, splice count, flicker rate, the counter running while the film that never arrives supposedly plays; a small gramophone disc turns while the tinny music-box ragtime loops, an original trifle composed for the booth. Tap advances the cards; the loop never delivers a film. Drag scrubs the frame counter through thousands of frames of nothing. Double-tap reseeds the booth numbers. "Leaving the pictures out of a film," Conrad said, "let me act on the body of the viewer." The bureaucracy is complete. The film is not coming. That is the film.

title: Outside the Dream
note: Outside the Dream Syndicate, 1972/73, Conrad with Faust: violin drones over a relentless pulse, the music nothing but interference. Four sine oscillators sit near 110 Hz, offset by fractions of a hertz, and their beats are drawn as concentric arcs at the center of a dark field: each ring breathes at one pair's beat rate, brightening as the waves reinforce, thinning as they cancel. The arcs are not a visualizer; they are computed from the same phase state that drives the oscillators, a measurement of the sound's grain. Tap to start the audio (it never autoplays) and switch on Faust's two-hertz pulse, ticked by the brass marker on the bar below. Drag sideways to detune: the beats accelerate, the rings churn, and on release everything settles back toward unison, the slow swell returning. Minimal, hypnotic, and honest: the picture is the interference, and the interference is the piece.

title: Loose Connection
note: Conrad's 1973 rig: a camera on baby-carriage wheels, rolling backward and forward while rotating, catching only a few frames at intervals. The street here is procedural and endless, flat storefronts with awnings and typographic signs, MUSIC, BOOKS, DELI, and the camera never stops its two motions at once: dollying along the street while the whole world slowly rolls. But you do not see the motion; you see the record: the display takes a frame roughly every third of a second and holds it, so the smooth journey arrives as a stutter of stills, the film catching every Nth moment of a trip that never pauses. Drag to take the wheel yourself, sideways for speed, up and down for roll; release and his programmed score resumes. Double-tap reseeds the street. The looseness is the connection: between the moving world and the frames that fail to keep up.

title: Four Square
note: Four Square, 1971: four projectors, four flicker films, one room. Four panels in a grid, each running its own black-and-white block map at its own rate, four drone strings in light. Left alone they beat against each other, alignments flashing and dissolving; every ninety seconds a conductor gathers them, rates and phases easing together until all four panels strobe as a single field, holds them a breath, then lets them drift apart again. Drag across a panel to push its phase: force an alignment, or break one that is forming. Double-tap reseeds all four maps. Every panel stays under the study's frequency cap; tap the top-right corner for the reduced-motion fades. Watch for the sync. When four projectors agree, the room itself seems to blink.

title: The Yellow Movie
note: A fifty-year film, finished the day it shipped. A sheet of paper, a hand-brushed black rectangle with one drip at the corner, and inside the frame a field of white house paint. That is the whole movie. The field is yellowing: seeded from its creation date, it drifts toward cream on a fifty-year curve, and the small label at the margin states the current frame, today 0.00 of 50 years. Nothing perceptible will change while you watch, or this year, or next; a visitor in a decade will meet a slightly different frame than you did. There is no interaction, because time is the interaction and it does not take requests. Conrad called these graphic works films because they project at the speed of chemistry. Stand here a moment anyway. Somewhere in the white, 2076 is developing.

title: Straight and Narrow
note: Conrad's 1970 film with Beverly Grant: successive frames of horizontal and vertical bars, and the heady moire they produce. Full-field bar frames alternate here at a capped rate, horizontal, then vertical, with a second pattern at 1.03 times the scale interleaved so the interference fringes crawl slowly across the field. None of the fringes are drawn; your visual system manufactures them, exactly as his audiences' did, the optical twin of the beat frequencies in his drone music. Drag tunes it: sideways for rate, up and down for bar width, like focusing a tuning fork. Double-tap reseeds the pattern. Tap the top-right corner, or use reduced motion, for a slow crossfade instead of the alternation. Ten minutes, a hard stop, and it begins again. The pattern is bars. Everything else is you.

title: Twenty Hertz
note: Conrad tuned his Flicker soundtrack synth to 20 Hz, the exact point where rhythm becomes pitch. This is the soundtrack without the film: a dark room, a small pilot lamp, a meter, and one sine oscillator sweeping slowly between 4 and 40 Hz. Below the brass threshold marker at 20 Hz the lamp resolves into separate flashes and the sound is clicks, a rhythm; above it the lamp steadies and the clicks fuse into a tone. Drag sideways to sweep the oscillator with your own hand and feel the crossing happen under your finger. Tap toggles between the fixed 20 Hz and the sweep. Sound starts only when you first tap, and there is nothing else to hear: no melody, no music, one oscillator doing physics at the border of two senses.

title: The Flicker Engine
note: Conrad's 1966 film, rebuilt honestly. It opens the way he opened it: a warning card, plain type on black, this film may be especially unsuitable for epileptics, a physician should be in attendance. Then the title frames, then nothing but black and white: block cycles engineered from his own diagrams, balanced counts, longer black on odd cycles, the whole screening arcing accelerate, dwell, decelerate, abrupt stop across about six minutes before the warning returns. The content is what your nervous system invents: phantom colors, shapes that were never rendered. Frequencies are capped at 14 Hz by construction. Double-tap starts a new screening with a new cycle map; tap the top-right corner (or set reduced motion on your system) and the strobe softens to a slow fade. The film has no pictures. It acts on the body of the viewer directly.

title: Athanor's Verbal Score
note: Athanor, 2025: at eighty, Chatham writes scores in prose now. "Play a flurry of notes." Three fragments of that notation drift on a warm dark ground: a flurry of notes, the choir enters, let it ring, set quiet as print. The piece waits for you, the way his rehearsals wait: "You can begin now." Tap a phrase and it ignites for six seconds, paying out its texture: the flurry bursts into red note-particles, the choir stacks its arcs, the ring expands its circles; drag a burning phrase and the texture smears behind your hand. Then the words cool back to parchment and can be lit again. Nothing plays itself. The score is only ever instructions until somebody begins.

title: Rêve Parisien
note: Paris, 2010: Chatham performed Rêve Parisien standing before Jacob Kassay's silvered paintings, the trumpet lines drawn over fogged silver. Two silver panels side by side, oxidation creeping their edges, a soft room ghosting in the metal; and across both, one thin electric-white trace: the trumpet phrase, redrawing itself every eight seconds, each version a new seeded arc. Drag and you walk past the paintings: the reflection field slides on both panels, the trace bends toward your passage, then everything relaxes home. Double-tap reseeds the phrases. The silver never sits still and the line never repeats. A duet for one instrument and one surface, each reflecting the other badly, beautifully.

title: The Loops of Nine, Ten, Eleven
note: Pythagorean Dream: Riley's technique, three tape loops of the same phrase at nine, ten, and eleven seconds. Three concentric rings, teal, rust, violet, and one bright motif riding each. The periods are exactly what the title says, never quantized to a common beat, so the copies drift: the nine-second ring gains a lap on the ten in ninety seconds, and the three will not agree again for sixteen and a half minutes. Drag draws a new seed phrase; on release all three loops take it up and begin their slow divorce, trails layering and blooming beyond their endpoints. Double-tap clears the slate bare. Sit long enough and the pattern you are sure you recognize dissolves; that dissolving is the composition working.

title: Fifteen-Second Cathedral
note: The Sacre-Coeur basilica gives back fifteen seconds of reverb, and A Crimson Grail was composed for exactly that: the building is the harmony. A field of simple stone-grey arches scattered on blue-black, three plain profiles, no church, no crosses, just the shape that holds sound. Touch one and it strikes: a gold glow blooms and decays over a full fifteen seconds, never shorter, because the fifteen seconds is the piece. Drag a phrase across several and they overlap into a luminous wash, each arch still ringing under the next. A slow ambient strike every seven seconds keeps the field breathing if you only watch. Strike one arch and count. The glow outlasts your patience, which is what cathedrals are for.

title: Antiphonal Compass
note: A Crimson Grail, Sacre-Coeur, 2005: hundreds of guitars placed around the audience, the motif handed from section to section around the ring. Here it is a plan view: eight emitter nodes on a brass-ticked compass ring, a dark void at the center where the audience sits, and a crimson pulse token traveling node to node, flaring at every handoff, its trail fading behind it; the center breathes once per full orbit. Drag in a circle and you conduct: the orbit takes your direction and speed, then decays slowly back to its resting circuit, one handoff every four seconds. Double-tap reseeds the motif's shape. No letters, no map, no guitars: the ring is the ensemble, and the music is the passing.

title: The Hidden Singers
note: "For my pieces with many electric guitars, people would come up after concerts and ask: where are you hiding the singers?" Nobody was hired. One thick low-E string crosses the lower third; struck, it raises its partials as pale arcs, two through sixteen; and as the gain climbs on a thirty-six-second loop, the arcs thicken and merge until their summed envelope stands up into a row of ghostly presences above the string, the choir the overtones brought with them. The figures are not drawn; they are the math, envelope lobes and cancellations standing shoulder to shoulder. They hold, they fade, the string is struck again. Listen with your eyes. The singers were in the string the whole time.

title: Dots (Don't Tell)
note: The dot system was Chatham's closely guarded secret: a guitar neck from above, dark board, two ivory dots glowing at the twelfth and fifteenth frets, and those dots are the score. Drag along the neck and the play-head travels the nodes, seventh, twelfth, fifteenth, nineteenth; arrive at one and it strikes, blooming concentric harmonic rings, partials two, three, five, seven, each ring's size and faintness set by its partial, expanding and fading over two and a half seconds. Underneath, a slow seeded riff keeps striking nodes on its own; double-tap and the riff reseeds to a new pattern. No numbers anywhere, no labels: the dots are the only marks, and knowing where to stop is the whole technique. Scrub slowly. The harmonics are brighter at the nodes, and the neck knows it.

title: The Tambura
note: Six strings, one note, fifty years: the all-E guitar of Guitar Trio, 1977, drawn as six pale lines on black. They are tuned almost, but not quite, together, and the almost is the music: interference between the micro-detuned strings shows as slow amber shimmer bands that travel along the lines, brightening where the waves agree, dimming where they quarrel. On a thirty-two-second loop the chord is struck, drifts and shimmers, settles toward near-unison as the bands slow and widen, fades, and is struck again with the next of three detune sets. There is no guitar, no hand, no pick: the lines play themselves. Chord is one; watch what it contains.

title: The Mouth
note: Greenpoint, 2014: Kassay strapped a billboard mechanism above a warehouse door, an enormous open mouth laughing silently over the street, advertising nothing. Here the mouth fills the frame as the painting it also was: poster-flat lips, a dark interior, brass teeth along both arcs, nine up, eight down, each slightly off true, because hands made them. On a sixteen-second loop it opens, holds, closes, holds: the slow silent laugh, teeth flashing as it opens. Tap and the timing reseeds, the laugh jumping to another point in its cycle and settling, because in this one piece the refresh is the artist's own joke and it belongs. No face, no sound, no product. Just the laugh, going nowhere, on schedule.

title: Khiropractik
note: A glass centipede in a red room: Kassay's contribution to the Bronx Zoo's World of Darkness, restaged as a slow anatomical study. Deep red walls, a low white plinth, a warm spotlight halo, and inside it the animal at rest length: twenty-six translucent segments, amber refraction along the lit edges, fine legs planted on the plinth, antennae forward. On a twenty-four-second loop the spine ripples with a traveling wave, the legs pulse half a beat behind it, and once a loop the head lifts, considers, and settles. There is nothing to do and nothing to fear: no horror, no scuttle, just articulation, patiently demonstrated. Watch the wave travel. A glass body makes the mechanics honest.

title: Candle Room
note: Candle Room: the light is the medium and the paintings merely report it. A dark industrial room, white columns, silvered canvases hung on them, a bronze slatted curtain rusting quietly under a beam, and exactly one source of light in the world: a candle flame low in the frame, flickering on a slow seeded rhythm. The silver faces catch it as warm patches that breathe with the flame; go near the screen and read the room by candlelight, the way the piece insists. Drag and you are weather: a gust leans the flame, the patches swing across the canvases, and everything settles back over a few seconds. Otherwise, watch. The darkness is most of the image, and it is not empty.

title: Footage
note: A tall panel of OSB, oriented strand board, the cheapest skin in building, carrying a photograph of itself: two procedural flake layers, the panel's actual surface and its own printed image laid on top, slightly darker, slightly off. At rest the misregistration is a whisper, eight pixels of doubt in the strands. Drag and the schism widens to thirty: every flake doubles, the depicted board sliding against the real one until the surface shimmers at two depths at once. The blue floor strip at the bottom keeps its counsel. Nothing else is depicted, because nothing else is needed: the actual and the image of the actual, failing to coincide. Slide it back to zero and feel the small relief of a thing matching itself, and how quickly the relief feels like a loss.

title: Codax
note: One painting, one color, one fictitious name: a square of saturated violet on white, signed quietly in the corner, h. codax. The color never changes. The hand does: drag and the surface scrubs between two makers, one enamel-smooth, the paint laid flat and clean as a factory finish; the other cloudy and oxidized, mottle blooming across the field, amber creeping the edges, the same violet gone weathered and doubtful. Release mid-scrub and the painting hangs between authors, half one hand, half the other. Nothing explains the device, because the device is the point: authorship as a surface treatment, identity as something a drag can revise. Leave it at the mixture you believe. The signature does not change either way.

title: The Stack
note: The 2009 debut, Eleven Rivington: a low white plinth in a dark room, and on it a stack of seven silvered panels lying flat, foggy silver faces up, tarnish creeping their rims, sheet edges layered at the sides. The stack is the composition, and it is yours to dismantle: drag across it and the top panel arcs off and leans beside the plinth, dark tarnished underside out; drag again for the next. Seven drags and the plinth stands empty, the panels fanned around it like a dealt hand. Double-tap and they file back into place, settling with weight. No orbit, no other view: the room is fixed, only the panels move. Take the stack apart slowly. Each underside is the silver's private face.

title: Burnt Edge
note: A square of silver, and time as chemistry: on a sixty-second loop the panel tarnishes in front of you, amber-brown oxidation blooming inward from the top, bottom, and left edges with an irregular, fingered front, the silver clouding as the stain advances, until the whole field sits deep in the plating bath's memory; it rests tarnished, then breathes back to clean silver and begins again. Nothing to touch, nothing to hurry: this is the metal remembering what was done to it. The creep is never a wipe and never geometric; it fingers and mottles like a real stain. Watch one full minute. The clean silver at the start of each loop feels less like a reset than like the panel forgetting, briefly, before it remembers again.

title: The Foggy Mirror
note: Kassay's silver painting, the mirror that refuses to mirror: one tall panel of electroplated canvas on a dark ground, its surface a fog in which a room barely exists: a bright window, a dark doorway, warm and cool weather, all blurred to the edge of disappearance, the canvas weave ghosting through the metal, amber oxidation creeping the top, bottom, and left edges like the bath remembering itself. The piece has no image of its own; it only reflects, badly, on purpose. Drag and the room slides across the silver, the window traveling farther than the doorway, exactly as turning your head in front of it would do. Leave it and the reflection drifts on its own. Stand still and let the fog decide what you look like.

title: A to Dot to Ring
note: The whole career in one line, three panels, three decisions: 1965, a bold black letter A on white, the young painter still signing his intentions; then the reduction, a single black dot, everything composition could be removed from, removed; then 1966, the ring, the outline that would repeat two hundred times and end a career's searching by refusing to search. The panels sit on one strip and you scrub it: drag horizontally to slide from A to dot to ring and back, the decisions staying separate, hard edges between them, no morphing, because history did not morph either. Release, and the view drifts home to the ring and rests there. Scrub backward once. Re-asking the reduction is the piece.

title: Two Orange Bars
note: The stripe program's endgame, from VNH Paris 2018: a wide white panorama and exactly two vertical orange bars, one at the quarter, one at the three-quarters, each an eighth of the canvas wide, standing in the void. The emptiness is the subject; the bars are almost an excuse. On a thirty-six-second loop they drift a few percent on slow independent sines, never leaving their zones, never meeting, never doing anything else. The ground stays absolute. If you are waiting for something to happen, you have misunderstood the piece in the most instructive way: the discipline is the work. Sit with the two bars. Measure the white between them with your eyes. That measuring is the painting happening.

title: Manifestation Five
note: December 1967, rebuilt as an engine: BMPT's motif-swap, one square canvas, one ring, three authors. For twenty seconds the ring is Toroni's: a circumference of cobalt brush imprints, jittering dabs where the outline should be. Hard cut: twenty seconds of Buren, the ring become an annulus of white and vermilion stripes at the 8.7 module. Hard cut: twenty seconds of Mosset himself, the flat black outline, administrative and calm. A tiny counter keeps the takes, 01/03, 02/03, 03/03, and the loop begins again. The motif never changes; the authorship rotates under it. Watch all three and decide which hand the ring belongs to. The group's whole argument was that the question is empty.

title: The Fold
note: Mosset's single allowance of illusion: a full field of even red and white horizontal stripes, and in the lower-right corner, a painted fold. At rest the corner lies flat, betrayed only by a hairline seam and a whisper of shadow. Drag, pulling toward the upper left, and the corner peels: the flat stripes turn a corner and become a striped box, the bands continuing unbroken across the fold edge onto the flap and the revealed underside, same pigment, new angles, with a soft shadow gathering underneath. It is not a real fold and never pretends otherwise for long: it is flat paint performing depth. Peel it slowly. The stripe continuity across the hinge is the whole trick, and it never breaks.

title: TBT
note: The chameleon diamond: a square canvas hung at forty-five degrees on a dark ground, painted in TBT chameleon pigment, whose color is not a property of the canvas but of where you stand. From one side it reads teal; shift, and it warms through copper; shift again, violet, the readings even spreading across the surface at once, teal lingering at one vertex while the other warms. Your movement is the pigment: drag horizontally and walk around it without moving, the hue easing after your hand like a material remembering. Leave it alone and it slowly cycles the viewpoints on its own, thirty seconds a tour. No rainbow, no effect: one coat of paint, three honest readings. Find the angle where it cannot decide.

title: Monochrome Field
note: The MDC Milano panorama at full scale: a vast vermilion-orange monochrome filling the frame wall to wall, flat even enamel with a whisper of grain and slightly darker edges. There is no motif and never will be. The only event is light: on a forty-second loop a specular sheen sweeps slowly across the surface and back, catching the enamel the way sun catches a car door, while the whole field breathes a few percent brighter and darker on the same slow phase. It must not become a gradient: it is a flat field with weather on it. Stand far back. Let the sheen make its crossing. The surface is the work, and the work is patience.

title: Diamond Presentation
note: The same ring canvas, one variable changed: the hang. The square hangs as a diamond, meeting the wall at a point instead of a side, its soft shadow pooling along the lower edges, and the painting itself is entirely unchanged. That is the experiment, and you run it: drag, and the canvas rotates continuously between square and diamond, any angle between, the ring riding rigidly inside its frame; let go, and it settles with a slow, weighty ease to the nearest honest orientation. Nothing else in the room moves. Presentation is the only content Mosset allows here, so present carefully. Turn it to the angle you would defend, and notice that the ring does not care.

title: The Ring
note: The canonical Mosset, drawn by a filing cabinet: a square white canvas, enamel-flat, and on it one black ring, an outline only, its stroke exactly 3.3 percent of the canvas, centered with a near-imperceptible drift. No brush texture, no expression: the hand is administrative. On a thirty-second loop the ring draws itself once, clockwise, thin to full; holds while a slow sheen crosses the enamel; then fades, and the filing starts again, each cycle's center and radius jittered by a hair, the way two hundred supposedly identical rings never quite are. Nothing to operate. Watch it be drawn. The most reproduced nothing in Swiss painting, reproduced once more, correctly.

The argument, split down the middle: on the left, 1965, the young painter composing, near-black ground, nested squares, sweeping vermilion and teal strokes, all gesture and decision. On the right, 1966, the decision that ended deciding: warm white, cobalt dabs at fixed intervals, the method that would hold for sixty years. A hard vertical line divides them, no blending, and the line is yours to move: drag it and re-decide the break, giving the painting more room or the method more wall; leave it alone and it breathes slightly, as if still thinking. No labels, no explanation: the piece is the argument. Slide the seam slowly and watch composition become system at the exact pixel where you stop.

title: The Ocean Answer
note: Why repeat the same grid for sixty years? Toroni's answer: you can look at the ocean every day, but it is never the same sea. Here is the proof, take by take: the identical cobalt lattice on warm white, twelve times in a forty-eight-second loop, four seconds a take, hard cuts between them like pages turning. The layout never moves a hair. The hand is never twice the same: pressure, rotation, paint load wander take by take, and a tiny counter in the corner, 01/12, 02/12, keeps the count so you can hunt the differences honestly. Fix your eye on one dab and ride all twelve takes. It is the same mark. It is never the same mark. That is the whole philosophy, demonstrated.

title: Column Study
note: The final support: three tall canvases stand floor to ceiling, the format of Toroni's 2025 Locarno retrospective, and down each one the imprints descend in a sparse vertical rhythm, green down the outer two, orange-red down the center. The viewpoint itself becomes the slow event: on a thirty-six-second loop the view drifts down the columns and back, the dabs passing like a meter stick being read, soft bands at top and bottom hinting that the canvases run on beyond the frame. Nothing else happens, and the monumentality is exactly that restraint: three columns of the same gesture, repeated at the scale of architecture. Stand in front of them. Let the drift carry your eye down and return it. The column is the last wall the brush ever needed.

title: Toile Cirée
note: The imprints on waxed fabric, Toroni's strangest support: a near-black ground with the oily sheen of toile ciree, and across it a dense brick-offset grid of ochre dabs, each with its bristle streaks and a thin gloss line where the brush landed. At one corner the fabric's folded hem turns under, a small triangle of material reality. The system itself never changes; what moves is the material: on a thirty-second loop a slow sheen wave crosses the field diagonally every twelve seconds, the oiliness traveling like light over a tablecloth, the dabs holding their intervals through it. Painted, never photographic. Run your eyes along a row and watch the sheen pass under the marks. The fabric breathes; the method does not.

title: Window Glass
note: Toroni on the street: a grid of dark glass panes in pale aluminum mullions at night, and on the center pane, painted directly on the glass as he did at the Swiss Institute, three white imprints that never move. Behind the glass the gallery glows faintly and breathes on a forty-second cycle, dim to bright and back, while reflection streaks slide slowly across the panes. That is all the motion there is, and it belongs to the light, not the marks: the imprints stay exactly where the brush left them while the city and the room take turns showing through. Stand outside and watch the window breathe. The support is the environment; the painting is three dabs of white holding still inside it.

title: The Red Doorway
note: The system-to-explore piece of the Toroni set: a white wall over a parquet floor, vermilion imprints climbing it in the regular brick-offset rhythm, and a doorway in the left third that the grid refuses to ignore: the rows bend around its frame, dabs bunching along the edges, none inside the opening. Two small canvases on the right carry black and orange imprints of their own. Now the experiment: drag the doorway sideways. It slides, and the entire field re-wraps around its new position instantly and mechanically, no bounce, no theatrics, the grid recomputing itself around the architecture in real time. Release it anywhere; the wall accepts the new arrangement as if it had always been so. The grid is the constant. You are the variable.

title: The Triangle
note: The grid meets architecture and gets clipped: a white gallery wall, a dark doorway centered in the lower half, and above it black imprints stacked in a triangle, one, two, three, up to seven, the regular lattice cut by the building's geometry into a measuring instrument. Inside the doorway, dimmer rooms hold small canvases with orange imprints, and their light slowly brightens and dims as if someone were passing through. On a twenty-four-second loop the triangle stamps itself in from the apex, dab by dab, holds, and fades. There is nothing to press: the wall is the system, the doorway is the variable, the triangle is the proof. Watch the apex land first. Everything else follows the interval.

title: Thirty Centimeters
note: The canonical Toroni, the whole method in one field: a warm-white ground and sixteen cobalt imprints of a single No. 50 brush, stamped at mechanically regular thirty-centimeter intervals in a brick-offset grid, floating sparse on the vast ground. Look close and each dab carries the hand: bristle streaks dense where the brush first pressed, drying toward the lift-off edge, a degree or two of rotation, a breath of scale difference. The placement never varies; only the touch does. On a thirty-second loop the field stamps itself in row by row, rests, and starts again on a fresh ground with a subtly different hand. Nothing to operate. Count the intervals; feel how the sameness refuses to be identical. That refusal is the painting.

title: Sail Race
note: A regatta of pure stripe: three tall triangular sails, white canvas banded red, green, and blue, crossing a flat warm-gray sea on parallel diagonal lanes, a horizon line low in the frame and nothing else, no hulls, no water, no wake but a faint echo of stripes trailing at fifteen percent. Their speeds stand in exact integer ratios over a forty-eight-second loop, so the blue laps the green, the green laps the red, overtakes happen mid-frame, and at the loop's close every sail is precisely where it began, ready to race again. Each sail billows on its own phase, canvas breathing. Wind, not motors. Pick a sail and follow it through an overtake; the crossing is the race, and the race never ends.

title: The Banner
note: The banner that got Buren's 1971 Guggenheim show cancelled, hung here at last: a giant double-sided striped banner drops from the top edge to eighty-five percent of the frame and divides it in two, the background halves differing by barely a tone. It sways on a thirty-six-second loop, breathing even at rest, and as it turns you catch the trick: the near face is white and red, the far face white and blue, and at the edge-on moment the faces trade, red giving way to blue like a flag changing allegiance. It never touches the bottom; it hangs, it divides, it turns. Watch a full sway and back. The most censored textile in conceptual art, finally flying indoors.

title: In Situ
note: The strictest recipe in the set: the frame itself is the site, and everything in the picture is measured off it. A vertical band of white and deep-blue stripes stands exactly one module in from the left edge and runs the full height; a second hugs the top-right corner like a blocked doorway; a third follows the frame's own diagonal, corner to corner. Nothing else exists. A small threshold block breathes at the bottom-right, but only when the frame is wider than tall: rotate to portrait and it simply is not there, a condition of the site, not a decoration. Resize the window and the bands slide to their new anchors, re-measuring themselves in a third of a second: the visual tool, laid down fresh each time. Placed, never composed.

title: Wild Posting
note: The affichages sauvages engine, 1967 forever: a stone-block wall with a shuttered doorway, and on it striped posters pasted bandit-style, white with red, blue, black, or yellow, at slight rotations, overlapping, clustered like they were put up at a run. The wall is alive before you arrive: five posters are already aging there. Drag across the wall and you paste a new one at your fingertip, snapped down, rotation from your drag's angle, color cycling the four. Every poster ages: after forty seconds a corner lifts, peels, and the poster fades away; the wall caps at twelve, oldest peeling first. There is no clear button and never will be: the wall does not reset, it turns over. Paste something. Watch it weather. The city is the gallery.

title: Observatory
note: L'Observatoire de la lumiere, the Fondation Louis Vuitton sails under Buren's filters: three curved glass sails sweep the frame at different scales, each a checkerboard of translucent colored cells alternating with white, cobalt, teal, orange, green, red, violet, yellow, magenta. A sixty-second day turns over them: at dawn and dusk the cells ignite in patches, one sail's edge burning magenta while another stays muted, lanterns against a deep sky; at noon everything washes pale under a near-white sky. No sun disc, no reflections, just flat color cells answering a moving light in sequence, never all at once. Forms appear and disappear by light, never by drawing. Stand under the sails and let the day pass.

title: Exploded Cabin
note: The Cabane Eclatee as a walk-through: six nested open frames of cream struts recede to a glowing vanishing point, each chamber infilled with flat translucent panes, red, orange, yellow, blue, violet, never opaque, so the chambers composite over each other and the color saturates with depth, yellows going olive over violet, oranges deepening over blue. Drag and you travel: the viewpoint pulls through the chambers, panes sliding past at their own rates, the layering thickening as you go; release, and the view settles softly back to the entrance. Untouched, it drifts in and out on a slow fifty-second breath. Light glows from the far end the whole way. Go in as far as the drag takes you; the corridor is the color, compounding.

title: Visual Tool
note: The outil visuel doing its one job: a plain neutral room, aggressively undecorated, flat floor, two walls, a ceiling line, a doorway, and across it, on a forty-five-second loop, one wide band of white-and-vermilion stripes sweeping left to right. The stripe decorates nothing; wherever the band passes, the room's edges ignite: corner, ceiling line, doorway frame flare white as if measured, and after the band moves on the edges remember the light for a few seconds, then forget. Nine seconds of plain room, then the tool crosses again. There is nothing to operate: the room is to behold. Watch the corner get found, lit, and abandoned. That is the whole theory of the work, demonstrated on architecture itself.

title: Two Plateaux
note: The Palais-Royal courtyard as a flat field: a diagonal grid of columns, every one striped black and white at the same unvarying module, tallest near the center, falling away along the diagonal to stumps, some running off the bottom edge into the buried lower level the real courtyard hides. Behind them the classical colonnade is a five-percent whisper; at the lowest columns' feet, dark water pools hold a few coin glints. The grid breathes on a forty-second tide, heights rising and falling in sequence along the diagonal, and if you drag, the columns shift in parallax, tall near, stumps far, exactly as your body would sort them. No color, no sky, no stone texture: the stripe module is the architecture. Walk the diagonal with your eyes.

title: Desert Draft
note: From the drawing years, when the work existed only on paper: a warm sheet, a faint grid, and a red-line architectural study of an unbuilt light environment drawing itself. Plan at bottom-left, side elevation above it, front elevation top-right, and the big aerial perspective center-right with its pyramid field and sight lines, plus the little title cartouche, all in thin red drafting lines with annotation marks that are pure gesture, never words. Each view draws in sequence, the completed sheet holds, fades, and a new study begins with different proportions, a different pyramid count, a different cove. Tap to re-draft on demand. Most of Wheeler's environments were never built; the drawing is not the plan for the piece. The drawing is the piece.

title: Center Light
note: The rare center-light variant, and the one Wheeler piece that lives on black: a dark room, and hovering in it a condensed glow with no frame, no panel, no edges, light dematerialized from its source and hanging in the space. White-hot core, blue-white inner aura, a deep blue-gray outer aura dissolving into the dark, a breath of grain in the lit air. This is the one piece where drag belongs: take the light and move it, the core following your fingertip with a soft lag, the aura trailing behind like disturbed water; let go, and over six seconds it drifts home to center and settles. No tap, no buttons, no hints: one gesture, discovered. The only bounded thing in the room is the light itself. Disturb it gently.

title: Sky Room
note: The 2020 blue room: walls, ceiling, and floor all washed in milky blue, and on the rear wall a rectangle of white light with soft bleeding edges, unbounded, not a window. The polished floor mirrors it honestly, the same glow flipped and squashed at forty percent, and at the rectangle's left a small seated silhouette keeps it company, dwarfed, the way visitors sit in the Zwirner photographs. The whole day breathes: on a slow fifty-four-second loop the rectangle swells and recedes almost imperceptibly while the room's blue deepens and lifts against it, dawn and twilight taking turns in a room with no outside. Nothing to operate. Sit where the figure sits. A clear day, indoors, breathing.

title: Rotational Horizon
note: The 2014 rotational horizon: a domed blue room, the floor gently convex like a piece of the earth, and ringing the floor a band of small LED points marking the horizon, shifting color ever so slightly, warm to cool to rose, in a slow traveling wave. One small dark figure stands at the center, on the high point. Drag and the room turns under your hand: the dome's light and the LED ring slide around you with wraparound, but the horizon curve and the figure stay exactly where they were, because that is the pilot's truth the piece is built on: the world turns, the horizon doesn't. Release and the rotation eases to rest. Take it for a spin, then let it settle, and watch the ring breathe color.

title: Aperture
note: The Bilbao story, built: a boy once walked into a Wheeler wall of light because he could not believe it was not solid. Phase one: a dark blue corridor, and at its end a doorway of pure white light so bright it reads as a wall. Tap, and you cross: a three-second push through the threshold, the bloom swelling to white-out, and then the fog room, light everywhere and from nowhere, drifting its slow dawn-to-dusk temperature. Tap again and you pull back out into the corridor, the rectangle shrinking to a doorway again. No frame, no hardware: the opening is light, and the crossing is the whole piece. Each tap is a small act of faith. Go through. Come back. Notice which side feels more real.

title: Anechoic Field
note: The floor of Synthetic Desert: a field of soft white pyramids, thousands of them, receding to a featureless void, and the only hard geometry Wheeler ever made, built to kill sound in a semi-anechoic chamber at the Guggenheim. Lit faces white, shadow faces blue-gray, and in the valleys between the tips a white daylight glow breathes: swelling and receding in slow traveling waves across the field, his molecular mist in constant flux. One dark platform floats at the right, and on it a single tiny figure, dwarfed, listening to the quietest room in art. The pyramids never move. There is nothing to operate. Stand on the platform in your mind and hear the field not make a sound.

title: Encasement
note: One of the 1967-69 Encasements: a vacuum-formed panel in a coved white room, its corners rounded away so the architecture never quite resolves. The panel itself is almost nothing, a slightly different white, but inside its edges runs a thin line of neon-bright blue-white, and from that line the glow bleeds outward in a soft halo until the panel seems to be dissolving into the wall that holds it. Drag and the light's fall shifts with your viewpoint, a small parallax in the halo. Tap and the panel changes temperature: white to blue to rose to white, crossfading slowly, the edge line re-tuning itself. The panel never moves. Only the light changes its mind. Stand in the cove and watch it fail to be an object.

title: Infinity Dawn
note: The infinity room with everything removed except the light itself: a full frame of near-white with no edges, no corners, no frame line anywhere, only a barely suggested floor curve at the bottom third and a breath of fine grain in the air. The one event is temperature: the room drifts through a slow cycle, warm rose dawn easing to neutral noon white, on to amber dusk, and back to dawn, cosine-smooth, never resting, so the field is always becoming a slightly different room. There is nothing to touch and nothing to operate. It is a room to inhabit for a minute, the way you would stand in his Zwirner installation while a half hour of artificial day passed over you. Move in. The light will do the rest.

title: Black Earth
note: Pure material: a black-glazed slab lying flat, filling the frame like a floor you are standing over, its whole surface finger-rippled under the glaze. No bands, no geometry, no image. The only event is light: a slow rake of illumination passes across the glaze every thirty-five seconds, and where the ripples' slopes align with it, the black answers with sheen, soft gray bands traveling over the surface, warming faintly at the glancing angles, the troughs staying pit black. Drag to carry the light yourself and feel the surface re-read itself under your hand. The slab never moves; the waves never move; only the light does, and that is enough to make the black inexhaustible. Look down and wait for the rake.

title: Night Torch
note: The sixty-foot inner-band painting on an exterior wall at night, nearly invisible in the dark: four wide vertical bands that are simply not there until light arrives. A torch you never see makes slow passes along the wall, resting, then sweeping: under its pool the band ignites gold-white, its microsphere grain suddenly legible, and behind the pool the band cools with a second-and-a-half afterglow before it dies back into the wall. Drag to carry the torch yourself; the bands you have lit keep their warmth a moment after you leave them. No cone, no flare, no hand: only activation, quiet as breath on a window. The painting spends most of its life unseen, and does not mind.

title: Blue Diamond
note: A square painting hung by one corner, and the blue is not paint: it is emitted light, cobalt microspheres retrieving the room's light and handing it back saturated. Diagonal brushwork sleeps in the blue until the field wakes. Down the middle runs a thin vertical white inner band, but the band and the field keep different hours: as your viewpoint travels, first the blue deepens and its grain condenses alive, and only later, at another station, does the white band flare to full brightness, so the light moves through the painting like a wave crossing water. It sways through those stations on a twenty-two-second cycle; drag sideways to walk the stations yourself. It is a painting, rotated. Stand where the blue is loudest, then go find the band.

title: Portal Arch
note: A single white arch on a black field, built the way she built them: a shortened band bent into two posts and a shallow lintel arc, no gothic point, no door, no scene behind it. The arch is a microsphere field, and it knows how far away you are. From far off it is a pale outline in the dark, a rumor of a doorway. Come closer and it fills with light from within, warming as it brightens, until the empty opening itself begins to glow, a doorway full of light with nothing on the other side. It drifts in and out on a slow twenty-five-second approach; drag upward to walk toward it, down to step back. Abstract as it is, your body will treat it as a threshold. Cross, or don't.

title: Electric Light
note: From the lightboxes of 1968, when she powered argon with a Tesla coil in the studio: a white slab hangs in a dark room on monofilament threads too thin to see, glowing with a spectral, sourceless light, brightest at its center, graying at the edges, its halo bleeding softly onto the wall behind. There is no lamp and no switch; the light simply is. It breathes on a slow forty-five-second cycle, and underneath the breath a faint mains flicker worries it, fast, tiny, irregular, the way real current behaves. Drag up or down to dim or brighten it yourself. The room stays dark. Sit with it the way you would sit with an aquarium: nothing happens, beautifully.

title: Glitter Black
note: Black as the ground that lets light read: a big black square dense with thousands of glitter points, framed by six small white microsphere squares, three down each side. The glints are not free to sparkle on their own; they answer to a warm pool of light drifting slowly across the field. Inside the pool they bloom, warm white with amber cores, a few throwing tiny cross flares; outside it they sink to near-invisible, five percent of nothing. Drag to carry the pool where you want it and watch the starfield wake and sleep under your hand. It is a starfield with a landlord: no light, no stars. Let the pool drift and the black does the rest.

title: White Light Field
note: Seven vertical bands of white and warm gray, full-bleed, and at first glance almost nothing: until the light moves. Each band is full of glass microspheres and gestural horizontal brushwork, but both stay invisible until the band's angle to the light is exactly right; then the band ignites from inside, warming toward gold, the beads and strokes suddenly legible, while its neighbors stay flat and quiet. The light sweeps slowly, thirty seconds across, so the bands flare one after another like a row of windows catching the sun in sequence. Drag to aim the light yourself and hold a band at its brightest. Monochrome plus light: the color was never applied, it is retrieved. Stand still and let the sweep come to you.

title: Inner Band
note: The painting that is only sometimes there. A large near-white panel hovers off a pale wall, and down its center runs a band of gray-taupe, except the band has a position where it lives: stand in the right place and it is a clear column of light, warm at its heart, its fine horizontal brushwork showing; step a few paces aside and it dissolves into the field until you would swear the panel was blank. The piece runs that walk for you: a slow twenty-second sway carries your viewpoint across the painting, the band kindling and vanishing, the panel's shadow shifting as you pass. Drag sideways to walk it yourself. Nothing is printed on the surface; the band is an event between the painting and your body. Wait for it to come back.

title: Standing Wall
note: Three tall panes of laminated glass stand in a white room, Venice Fog colors: Sea Salt mist, lapis, French blue, each pane translucent, each tinted further by its angle to the light. But the piece is the arithmetic: where two panes overlap on screen, the color is the true product of the two laminates, lapis through mist giving steel blue, French blue through lapis giving deep indigo, computed geometrically, not faked with transparency. Drag and you walk around the wall: the panes swing in parallax, the overlaps grow and shrink, the shadow on the floor shifts its tint. Left alone it orbits slowly on its own. Stand in front of it, then step aside, and watch the blues multiply.

title: Gas on a Puddle
note: His own words for the coating: the same phenomena as seeing a little gas on a puddle at a filling station. So here is the stain itself, abstract and flat: an irregular dark blob on asphalt gray, and inside it the thin-film rainbow cut down to Bell's narrow register, concentric bands of violet, gas gold, teal, one passage of magenta, cresting and dissolving into the near-black base instead of ending in hard rings. The film breathes on a forty-second cycle, spreading, thinning, contracting, the bands rippling inward as it grows. Tap the film and you stir it: ripples run out from your touch and scatter the bands, settling over eight seconds. Drag to smear it. Narrow bands, dark field, restraint: that is the whole effect, and it is enough.

title: Mirage
note: His early-eighties heat-and-light illusion, rebuilt from what it actually was: not temperature but stacked transparencies. A pale sky, a dark warm ground, and just below the horizon line, the mirage band: seven translucent film strips, amber, glare white, mirage blue, waving like air over hot asphalt. The color is strongest at the mirage line itself and dissolves as the strips step away from it, and where strips overlap they brighten, the way layered Mylar does. The shimmer runs on an eighteen-second loop built from integer-ratio sines, so it closes on itself exactly and breathes forever without repeating a seam. Nothing to touch: this is a heat phenomenon, not a toy. Watch the horizon shiver.

title: Vapor Drawing
note: From the Vapor Drawings, 1978 onward: thin-film coating on paper, and paper changes the rules, because it cannot transmit, only reflect and absorb, so the work goes darker, flatter, sootier than the cubes. Over a black-brown soot ground, inside a thin float frame: a stepped column of amber warming to paper white down the center, a cluster of torn Mylar shards center-right, blue-gray film strips with ripped edges and small gold interference ticks, and one large white paper shard lower-left that reads as a hole cut straight through the dark. A slow heat-haze shimmer runs across the layers, under two pixels, like warm air over a surface. Press a shard and hold, and it lifts a breath off the ground. The edges are the detail: everything here is torn, nothing is cut clean.

title: Floating Volume
note: The cube again, but this time the subject is the space under it. Bell's cubes sat on clear pedestals so they seemed to float on the light between the floor and the work, and this one does: no visible support, just the interference glass hovering in the upper room and, on the floor beneath, a soft pool of colored light whose hue is whatever the cube's faces are doing right now. The float is a pure slow sine, a few pixels over twelve seconds, no bounce, and the pool breathes against it: as the cube rises the pool tightens and dims, as it sinks the pool spreads and deepens. The light orbit turns over ninety seconds behind everything. Drag to move the light; never the cube. It weighs nothing. Watch it hover.

title: Corner Play
note: A nod to the childhood corner he never stopped loving: three coated-glass faces meeting at a single corner, filling the frame edge to edge, and the faces themselves are pale and ghostly, near-white with the faintest interference tints. The corner is the star. Where the three panes meet, the coating densities stack, and the seam burns: gold at its brightest near the corner knot, falling away to violet at the far ends. A hotspot of light travels the seam over a three-minute orbit, so the corner seems to ignite, dim, and ignite again, while the faces barely shift. Drag to move the light azimuth yourself. Restraint is the point: one bright seam in a white room. Watch the corner catch fire, slowly.

title: Three States
note: His dictum, built as one pane of glass filling the frame: glass reflects, transmits, and absorbs, all at the same time, and here the three states share a single surface. On the left the pane is a mirror, silver-blue with a bright mirrored streak. In the middle it is a window, warm light, and the dim gallery behind reads clearly through it, arch glow, plinth, far wall. On the right it is soot, deep graphite with a violet undertone, swallowing the room to a ghost. The bands bleed into each other along iridescent seams, violet sliding to gold, dusted with film grain. Drag sideways to push the boundaries: widen the mirror and its streak deepens; widen the window and the view clears. The pane breathes on its own between your visits.

title: Interference Cube
note: One cube, one coating material, and at any moment three different colors: a gold face, a violet-gray face, a near-white top, none of them painted. That is thin-film interference, Bell's whole career in one object: the color lives in the angle between you and the light, not in the glass. Each face is doing all three of his tricks at once, a mirrored streak for reflection, a hue-shifted wash for transmission, a darkening floor for absorption, and where two panes meet the seam glows brighter than either face. The lights orbit slowly so the colors cycle on their own, prism unlocking and re-locking. Drag to tilt the light yourself and walk the faces through the interference range. It never sits still because the color was never in the cube.

title: Fractured Wire
note: Fractured Light, MoMA 1970: a plain room cut by hairline stainless wires that appear to float. They can float because their attachment points are painted white, vanishing into the wall, and each wire gives up in the middle, fading to nothing mid-span before it remembers itself at the far wall. A translucent scrim band hangs across the upper third. Underneath it all, the room's light slowly trades temperature: over a four-minute cycle the warm wash rises to dominance and the wires go crisp, then the cool wash takes over and the wires ghost away, then back again. No fixtures, no switches, nothing to do. The ordinariest room, made strange by light alone. Stand in it until the wires disappear.

title: Always Changing
note: The Getty Central Garden as a system, mantra included: always changing, never twice the same. A stream pours down stepped chadar stone from the upper left, brightening at every drop, splashing white at the step edges, gathering in the bowl pool at lower right where the azalea maze floats: three interlocking circles of green. Rebar bowers thick with bougainvillea frame the top corners. The maze's bloom keeps the real season, read from the date: today, late autumn, the rings are sparse with a few pink holdouts; come spring they flare solid pink, and in winter they go bare. Drag upstream and you dam the flow for a moment; let go and the backed-up water surges through. The flow itself is seeded so it never visibly repeats. Stand by the stream a while.

title: Excursus Square
note: Homage to the Square, cubed: four nested squares and nothing else, no outlines, no shadows, the bands separated only by the chromatic edge itself. But the bands are instruments, not colors on a chart: over a six-minute drift each band's hue wanders a few degrees on its own slow cycle, the value ladder held steady, so the relationships keep reorganizing: the rust band advances, then recedes; the deep slate center sinks, then floats. An Albers study rebuilt as a time piece, after his Excursus at Dia. Double-tap and the whole stack reseeds to a new family of muted ochres, rusts, creams and slates, crossfading over four seconds. Nothing rotates, nothing scales: only color moves. Watch one band until it changes its mind about its neighbors.

title: Fluorescent Fold
note: Light and Space, 2007, and the Sunshine Noir trick: two fields of fluorescent tubes, one behind the other at a thirty-degree cross-hatch, tubes wrapped in theatrical gels and ticked with black and white tape, so plain white light fractures into tonal fields no pigment could mix: fissures of violet, teal, amber and rose running the length of the tubes. The layout is irregular, never a grid, and there are no fixtures or sockets to look at: light as material, not a picture of light. Each tube's gels slowly drift in hue over five minutes, so the fractured fields breathe. Drag across the piece and the whole tube field bends gently under your finger, then settles straight when you let go.

title: Dawn to Dusk
note: Untitled (dawn to dusk), his largest work, a former hospital wing at Chinati built around the sun: a room cut in two by a vertical scrim, one half engulfed in light, the other held in dark, and the boundary between them sweeping across the room as the real sun crosses the real sky. This version runs on your local time, by the minute: at dawn the light half is born at one wall with the boundary glowing amber; by noon the room has turned itself inside out; at dusk the dark takes the room back, and at night both halves go deep. No sun disc, no landscape, no clock readout: a clock that never tells time. Open it at different hours and it is a different room.

title: Scrim Dissolve
note: Squaring the Circle by way of the Whitney scrim veil: a plain white room, and across its left third a floor-to-ceiling scrim of translucent fabric. Behind the scrim, the far corner has been quietly edited: the wall there truly curves, but through the fabric it reads squared, and slightly out of focus, and the only evidence is a faint tension line down the cloth and a leak of warmer light at its far edge. Nothing announces the trick. Over an eight-minute cycle the leak swells and fades and the tension line drifts in and out of legibility, so the anomaly is noticeable for a while, then gone, then noticeable again. The piece is the moment you notice. Watch the corner until it looks wrong.

title: Dot Field
note: The dot paintings: from across the room, a blank off-white canvas, nothing on it at all. Lean in, and it is covered in minute green and red dots, hundreds of them, each placed by hand, denser toward the middle, and once your eye finds them they will not sit still: they dance and lift off the surface, the hide-and-seek color play he built in 1964. Scroll or pinch to lean in here: the dots emerge and start their dance, then subside back under the threshold when you let go. Drag through the field and a wake of dancing follows your finger, settling over about ten seconds. Double-tap and the canvas blanks, then a new arrangement of dots settles in. From a distance: nothing. Up close: everything.

title: Disc Float
note: Irwin's disc paintings, 1966 to 69: a convex aluminum disc floating against a wall painted almost the same off-white, so the disc has no edge of its own and reads only through the shadows it throws. Four hidden light sources cast overlapping shadow arcs behind it, and where the arcs cross they leave a luminous quatrefoil, the glowing four-petal shape in which the disc loses itself and hovers. The disc never moves: the LIGHTS orbit, slowly, over three minutes, so the shadows swing and the disc seems to rise and sink in indeterminate space. Drag to shift the light yourself. Press and hold, and the rig fades to plain natural light: the shadows die, and the disc dissolves entirely into the wall. Hold again to bring the lights back.

title: Dissolve Wall
note: Dissolve, from the Curved Glass series: a wide, rounded aperture cut in a dark wall, and behind its curved glass a slow LED program breathes color, deep blue to cyan to magenta to amber to deep red, each color holding while the wall around the aperture picks up the same tint, so the whole room seems to breathe with it. No LED strips, no reflections, no names for the colors: the apparatus stays hidden and the wall simply glows. Honest note: the real program runs an hour, each color holding eight to ten minutes; this version plays his own compressed four-minute preview cycle, the same mechanism at a gallery-friendly period. Watch a full cycle if you can; the red at the end is worth it.

title: Meeting Roof
note: Meeting, MoMA PS1: a square hole jackhammered out of a concrete ceiling, and the edge is the signature, raw, chipped, broken concrete, never a clean cut. Through it, a flat plane of sky runs its own daylight program on your real local time. Around it, the ceiling takes the second color system: his 2016 LED program, washing the concrete in rose, teal and amber in the hour around sunrise and sunset, strongest at the rim, so the artificial light and the natural sky meet exactly at the broken edge, the meeting of the space inside with the space of the sky. At night both systems rest and the aperture holds a deep blue dark. There is no clock and nothing to press. Be there at dawn.

title: Alpha Tunnel
note: Roden Crater's Alpha Tunnel as an instrument you look through: a long stone corridor in one-point perspective, course rings shrinking toward the Image Stone at the vanishing point, a pale shaft of light falling from the tunnel mouth, dust drifting in it. The stone is a camera obscura, and what it shows is computed from the real date, nothing else: in the southernmost-sunset window, December 11 to 31, the sun's image burns on the stone at the position the declination dictates; near a major lunar standstill it holds a dim moon; the rest of the year, like today, it shows near-darkness and a faint outline, exactly as the real tunnel would. No label names the date or the event. The piece is the instrument. Watch the dust; come back in December.

title: Hind Sight
note: Dark Space: the screen begins pitch black, and it means it. Over ten minutes a faint luminous doorway rises from below the threshold of vision, following the real curve of dark adaptation, fast in the first three minutes while your cones adjust, then slow as the rods take over, breathing once at the halfway point. At full rise the form is still barely there, a whisper of blue-gray at a few percent of light, and then it fades back to black and the cycle begins again. There is no skip, no timer, no tap to reveal: he charges ten minutes of darkness for a glimpse, and this version keeps the price. Sit with the black until the doorway finds you.

title: Wedgework Drift
note: Two blades of projected light crossing in a dark room, one Key Lime, one violet, slicing the black at angles. Where they cross, the brightness adds, and at the extremes of their slow drift the room itself gives up: the faint corner seam fades to nothing and the walls read as if they extended past their own bounds, which is the whole Wedgework effect, architecture dissolved by light. The blades pivot and settle over a seamless minute, clean, no dust, no visible source. There is nothing to touch; the dissolve is the performance. Watch the room come apart at the crossing.

title: Afrum Corner
note: His 1966 trick, the one that started everything: a flat polygon of warm white light projected into the corner of a dark room, and because the projection folds exactly on the corner line, your eye assembles it into a luminous cube hovering just off the wall. There is no cube. There is only light with, in his word, thingness. The projection breathes faintly, like a projector lamp. Tap, and the hidden projector re-aims: the corner shifts, the fold re-forms, and the cube hangs in its new place. No apparatus is ever shown. Tap to re-aim the light, then look until the cube floats.

title: Ganzfeld Clear
note: The Ganzfeld, engineered at screen scale: an edgeless field of pure color with no frame, no horizon, no texture, nothing for the eye to hold onto, so the screen stops reading as a surface and starts reading as a place you are inside. The field runs a twelve-minute cycle of color baths, turquoise, magenta, amber, violet, each holding for minutes with a slow breathing in its brightness, then softening into the next. Once per cycle, in the middle, a single soft white strobe blooms and dies. No controls, no progress, no skip: the piece requires the one thing Turrell always charges, which is time. Stand in the color and wait.

title: Skyspace Dawn
note: A knife-edge aperture cut in a dark stone ceiling, and through it a plane of sky so flat it feels within reach: no clouds to speak of, no horizon, just color held at arm's length. The piece runs on your real local time. In the forty minutes around sunrise it plays the dawn program, pre-dawn rose warming through amber to pale sky; around sunset it runs the sequence back down; the rest of the day the sky simply holds a still noon flatness with a barely-there drift. There is no clock, no readout, and nothing to press: Turrell asks for sustained looking, so that is all there is to do. Watch the light change at the speed of the morning.

title: Dream Blots
note: Rorschach blots in the colors of dreams, which cannot be verified, and the caption says so: dream color, unverified. One large blot at a time, on aged paper, drawn in a single dream color from his fixed sequence: dusty rose, deep teal, ochre, slate violet, moss, ember. Each blot draws itself at the fold: the left half appears as overlapping ink masses with wobbled, imperfect outlines, because a perfect ellipse was never dreamt, then the right half unfolds as its exact mirror. It holds, fades, and the next dream comes in its turn. Double-tap to skip to the next dream. There is no reseed and no explanation of what any blot looks like. Watch them come and go.

title: Rose Window
note: Morning light through the rose window at Saint-Denis, rebuilt honestly in LED: twelve glowing tubes radiate from a dark hub, five blues, three yellows, two reds and a pink, their colors pooling in a soft wash on the wall behind them, exactly the way the real installation reads across a dark gallery. The wheel breathes, barely. Drag to rotate the whole mandala slowly, wash and all. Tap a tube and it pulses and retunes one step, always staying inside its own color family: a blue stays blue, a yellow stays yellow. No stained-glass leading, no chaos: the order holds, and the light changes only by turning. Drag to turn the morning.

title: Goldberg Fixtures
note: Fourteen tall fluorescent fixtures in a row, seven for the left hand and seven for the right, standing dark on near-black, and a melody you watch instead of hear: an original two-voice counterpoint is composed fresh by the piece, phrase by phrase, and each note lights its fixture in the color Isaac Newton assigned that pitch, red for C through violet for B. Notes hold their glow for exactly their duration, warming up and cooling down the way real fluorescents do, never snapping. The readout at the bottom keeps the variation count. Tap a fixture and its voice takes the next phrase solo. The light is the music; there is no sound.

title: Walden Rope
note: His Walden Pond soundings, after Thoreau: a long hemp rope sagging across dark water-black, carrying paper tags at intervals, and each tag holds a depth figure and a small hand-wobbled watercolor swatch color-matched to the water at that sounding, greens darkening with depth. About forty tags ride the rope at once, swaying gently; the readout at the top-left keeps the current depth and the pond's coordinates. Drag down to lower the sounding line: the rope dips, the readout deepens, fresh tags slide in at the leading edge and the oldest detach at the trailing edge. Release and the line eases back up. Neither entirely documentation nor sculpture. Drag to sound the pond.

title: Cosmic Latte
note: Cosmic Latte: the average color of the universe, a warm yellowish white, hung indoors as a night sky. Six hundred small bulbs arch across the gallery black in the gentle curve of the Milky Way, and they are clustered the way pigment molecules cluster: big sparse titanium-white knots, medium Mars-yellow and chrome-yellow ones, and tiny rare cadmium-red sparks, three percent only. The whole arch crawls almost imperceptibly, sidereal, and each bulb breathes a little on its own phase. No blue, no cool white, no constellations: the warmth is the entire point, and the brightness stays low, like a gallery after hours. There is nothing to touch. It is a sky. Watch it breathe.

title: September Blues
note: Trying to Remember the Color of the Sky on That September Morning: a full-bleed grid of hand-painted watercolor squares on warm paper, nearly a thousand tiles, every one a slightly different blue and nothing else, ever. Each tile is laid in overlapping brush strokes with wobbling edges and uneven fill, so the hand shows in every square. Once a minute a slow wet wave crosses the field: tiles near the front briefly deepen and saturate, as if freshly painted, then dry back. Tap a tile and it holds wet for five seconds. The grid never reseeds and never decorates itself; it stays fixed and quiet, like his. Watch the wave pass.

title: River Panes
note: The River That Flows Both Ways, rebuilt as a window wall: behind the glass, a slow abstract river pans by, dark water in layered bands with pale light streaks drifting. Every half second the exact center of the scene is sampled and locked into the next pane as a glowing purple-grey square; the panes grow from the top-left, grout lines and all, until the wall is full at about seven hundred panes, hold, then clear row by row and begin again. The colors never leave the purple-grey family he mixed for the Hudson, so the wall reads as glass, not a photograph. A thin readout keeps count. Tap anywhere to force a sample now and jump the queue.

title: Moonlight Tube
note: The colorimeter protocol at its most condensed: one horizontal fluorescent tube floating on near-black, built from nine flat gel bands, warm amber through cool blue to pale violet, over a bright core, its light spilling softly on the wall behind. The tube holds the exact color of a full moon over Luna County, New Mexico, and it runs the whole lunar month in twenty-eight seconds: full bright at the start, dimming day by day to a faint ghost at mid-loop, never quite black, then waxing back to full. The caption underneath keeps the measurement honest: the place, the phase day, the derived kelvin, all moving with the light. Tap the tube to snap it back to full moon. The tube is the moon; there is no sky.

title: The Well
note: Well: a paper coffee cup with no bottom, floating over a dark circular well of water, stark and diagrammatic. Tap to drop a coin: it falls with a slight wobble straight through the cup, out the open bottom, and into the water, where a ripple rings outward and fades. Each coin joins a growing field of glints on the water, and one of three ledgers at the base ticks up with a small stamp: DESIRING, SAVING, DONATING, weighted half, a third, a fifth.
